record_type_quote: The claim selected for replication from de Langhe et al (2014) is the Study 2 claim that consumers base their predictions of quality given price on perceived covariation, in particular the presence of a price region where quality is locally consistent increases the predicted quality at high price: experiencing consistently low quality products at lower prices should lead to more extreme price-based quality predictions at higher prices.

targets.authors: de Langhe, B., van Osselaer, S. M. J., Puntoni, S., & McGill, A. L.
targets.title: Fooled by Heteroscedastic Randomness: Local Consistency Breeds Extremity in Price-Based Quality Inferences.
targets.evidence_quote: The claim selected for replication from de Langhe et al (2014) is the Study 2 claim that consumers base their predictions of quality given price on perceived covariation, in particular the presence of a price region where quality is locally consistent increases the predicted quality at high price: experiencing consistently low quality products at lower prices should lead to more extreme price-based quality predictions at higher prices.
targets.outcome_quote: Thus, the focal hypothesis was replicated. The test of the secondary hypothesis (H1) is given by the Price X Condition: Variance Decreasing interaction term (delta-1b). Here we found a non-significant interaction, with b = 0.03, SE = 0.08, t(513.04) = 0.37, p = 0.709, indicating that the regression slope for price in the condition where quality was consistent at high prices was not reliably different from the condition where quality was never consistent.
targets.outcome_reasoning: The original claim is explicitly described as steeper slopes for both locally consistent conditions. The focal low-price effect replicated while the tested high-price effect did not. Successful replication of the focal hypothesis is a verdict on that comparison, rather than the whole two-hypothesis attempt.
